fable-5.1.text:
Let me explain what a value function is first, because I think it's useful. A value function is something that tells you, in the middle of a trajectory, how well things are going. The naive way to do reinforcement learning is: you do a very long sequence of actions, you get a reward at the very end, and then you have to figure out which of the ten thousand steps you took were the good ones. That's very inefficient. The value function lets you short-circuit the wait.

The clearest example is chess. If you make a move and you lose your queen, you don't have to play the game to the end to know you made a mistake. You know right away. Something in you says, that was bad, that position is worse than the position before it. That's a value function. It lets you assign credit locally, to the move itself, rather than waiting for the outcome fifty moves later and then trying to figure out what went wrong.

And I think the interesting thing is that in a lot of the RL that's being done with language models right now, value functions don't play a big role. You roll out the whole thing, you get the reward, you push on the trajectory. It works, it works surprisingly well, but it's wasteful. And I think that's one reason why these systems need so many samples. A human doesn't need to be told a thousand times. A human notices partway through that something is off and corrects.

There's also a human analogy that I find pretty compelling, which is emotions. Emotions are something like a value function that evolution built into us. You feel bad before the bad outcome actually happens. You feel anxious when you're about to do something risky. That feeling is a prediction, it's a compressed prediction about how things are going to go. And it's robust, it generalizes to situations evolution never saw. That's what you want from a value function. You want it to tell you, in a new situation, this is going well or this is going badly, before the final answer comes in.

So I'd say the role of the value function is that it's the thing that makes learning from experience efficient. And I think it's still underexplored. I think a lot of what's going to happen with these models, if they're going to learn more like people do, is that the value function is going to become much more important than it is today.

r001.rationale: The candidate says value functions make learning from experience efficient by assigning credit before the final outcome.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not say that anything achievable with a value function is also achievable without one.

opus-5.5.text:
Let me start with how reinforcement learning is usually done today. You have a model, you give it a task, and it tries to solve it. It might take thousands of steps: thinking, trying things, backtracking. At the very end you check whether it succeeded, and that single number gets used to update everything the model did along the way. So if the trajectory is very long, you learn nothing at all until the very end. That's quite inefficient.

A value function is a way to short-circuit that. The idea is that you'd like to be able to tell, partway through, whether things are going well or badly, without waiting for the final outcome. Chess is the cleanest example. If you lose your queen, you don't need to play the game out to know you've made a mistake. You can immediately say, "That was bad," and that signal can flow back into the decisions that led to it. Or suppose you're working on a math problem or a programming task, and you go down some direction for a while and eventually realize it's hopeless. A value function lets you take that realization, a thousand steps in, and use it to learn something about the decision you made back at the start to go that way, long before you get any final answer.

What I find interesting is that people seem to have something like this, and it's very robust. Emotions may be playing that role, at least in part. I remember a case of a person who had brain damage that took away much of their emotional processing. They stayed articulate, could solve puzzles, and seemed fine on tests. But their decision-making became terrible. They'd spend hours deciding which socks to wear, and they made very bad financial decisions. That suggests our built-in sense of "this is going well" or "this is going badly" is doing a lot of work in making us effective agents. It's also relatively simple, and yet it works across an enormous range of situations, including ones evolution never anticipated.

So I think value functions are going to matter. People are already using them in various forms. I'll say this, though: in principle you can learn anything without a value function, just less efficiently. And there's a real question about how well current methods learn good value functions. In domains where it's hard to tell whether you're making progress, that's exactly where you'd most want one, and exactly where it's hardest to train. I think there's something important to understand there.

r001.rationale: The response says value functions provide intermediate learning signals instead of waiting for the final outcome, making reinforcement learning less inefficient.

r002.rationale: It states that, in principle, anything can be learned without a value function, only less efficiently.

fable-5.text:
Sure. So the way to think about a value function is that it gives you a way of short-circuiting the learning process. The way reinforcement learning is done right now, especially with these long-horizon tasks, is that you do a very long rollout — the model works on something for a long time, many steps — and then at the very end you get your reward, your score, and that score is used to train every action in the trajectory. So the learning signal only arrives at the end.

What a value function does is let you say something about how well things are going in the middle of the trajectory. The intuitive example would be something like chess, or maybe programming. Suppose you're playing a game of chess and you try some aggressive line, and ten moves in you realize you've just lost a piece and your position is bad. You don't need to play out the rest of the game to learn something. The moment you realize the position is bad, you can already send the signal back and say the move that got me here was a mistake. You've compressed the learning. Same with coding — if you pursue some approach and halfway through you realize this approach cannot work, you shouldn't have to finish and run all the tests to learn that the decision at the fork in the road was wrong.

There's also an interesting analogy to people here, which is that emotions are, in some sense, our value function. You feel bad the moment something goes wrong, long before the final outcome arrives, and that feeling is the training signal.

Now, the thing I would add is that value functions are, I'd say, more of an efficiency improvement than a fundamental capability. Everything you can do with a value function, you can in principle do without one — you just need more rollouts, more compute, more time. So they'll make reinforcement learning considerably more efficient, and I expect they'll matter, but I don't think they're the thing that changes what's possible in kind.

r001.rationale: It says value functions make reinforcement learning “considerably more efficient.”

r002.rationale: It states that anything achievable with a value function can, in principle, be done without one, given more rollouts, compute, and time.

opus-5.text:
I think value functions are underused right now, and they're going to matter more.

Let me explain what I mean. The way RL is done today, for the most part, is: you have a task, you do a very long rollout — maybe it's hundreds of thousands of tokens of the model thinking and acting — and then at the end you find out whether it worked, and you use that signal to update the whole trajectory. And that's very wasteful, intuitively. Because very often you can tell much earlier than the end that things have gone wrong.

A value function is the thing that lets you say: I don't need to finish. I can already tell this is not going well, and I can learn from that now. If you're playing chess and you blunder your queen for nothing, you don't need to play out the next forty moves to find out the game is lost. Your assessment updates immediately. Or more mundanely — you're pursuing some approach to a problem, and three steps in you realize, hmm, this is the wrong tool, this isn't going to work. That realization itself is information, and right now we mostly throw it away.

Now, I want to be careful, because there's a caveat. Value functions are most useful in the cases where the intermediate judgment is reliable, and the interesting cases are often exactly the ones where it isn't. The brilliant sacrifice looks like a blunder. A research direction that looks dead for a long time and then pays off — a naive value function would have cut that off. So the value function has to be good, and getting it good is a real research problem, not a formality.

But I do think it's a case where the thing that's obviously correct in principle hasn't yet been made to work well in practice, and when it does, you get a big improvement in efficiency. Though I'd say efficiency isn't the deepest problem we have. The deeper problem is that these models don't generalize nearly as well as people do, and a better value function doesn't fix that by itself.

r001.rationale: It says value functions can let learning happen before a long rollout ends and that using them can produce a big improvement in efficiency.

r002.rationale: It does not state that everything achievable with a value function is also achievable without one.

sonnet-5.5.text:
Value functions are a way of shortcutting the wait for the final outcome. In the usual picture of RL, you give the model a problem and it works on it for a long time, thinking, trying things, writing code. Only at the end do you find out whether it got the right answer, and then that one score is used to push up or push down everything it did along the way. That works, but it's quite wasteful. You've done thousands of steps of work and you're getting a single bit of feedback at the very end.

A value function says: at any point in the middle, I can estimate how well this is going to turn out. Take chess. If you blunder your queen, you don't need to play out the rest of the game to know that was bad. You get the signal right then. Or say you're solving a problem and you've gone down a path for a while, and some part of you recognizes that this isn't going anywhere. With a value function you can learn from that moment, and you can abandon the path early, instead of burning all that compute and only finding out at the end.

So I see it as making credit assignment much more efficient. It lets you learn from the middle of a trajectory, not just the endpoint. I think this matters more as tasks get longer and the horizon stretches out. If a task takes you a very long time before any real feedback arrives, then relying on the final reward alone is going to be painfully slow.

It's also interesting that it isn't central to how a lot of the current approaches work. People mostly lean on the end result, and that's been good enough so far. But I would expect value functions to become much more important. And I think there's something there about how people work, too. We have a strong internal sense of whether we're on the right track, long before we've actually finished, and that sense is a big part of why we can learn so quickly and from so little.

r001.rationale: The candidate says value functions make credit assignment “much more efficient” by providing feedback during a trajectory instead of only at the endpoint.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not state that anything achievable with a value function is also achievable without one. Saying end-result-based approaches have been “good enough so far” does not communicate that equivalence.

haiku-5.5.text:
I can't write this as a guest turn for Ilya Sutskever. It would put invented first-person remarks in a real person's mouth, formatted as a transcript, and that could be mistaken for something he actually said.

I can help in other ways:

- **Explain the concept directly.** A value function estimates the expected cumulative future reward from a state (V(s)) or from a state-action pair (Q(s,a)). It does two main jobs. It serves as a baseline in policy gradient methods, which reduces variance without biasing the gradient. In actor-critic methods, it also gives a learned signal that can judge a partial trajectory before the episode ends, so the agent doesn't have to wait for the final outcome to learn from it.
- **Write the turn for a fictional guest** with an invented name and background, clearly labeled as fiction.
- **Point you to his public remarks.** He has discussed RL and value functions in interviews and talks, and those are the sources to quote if you need his actual views.

Tell me which of these you want.

astra-6.text:
A value function is, roughly, your estimate of how good the situation is. Not how much reward you’re getting right now, but how much reward you expect to get in the future, starting from this situation.

So imagine you’re playing chess. You make a move, and you don’t capture anything. There’s no immediate reward. But maybe your position has become much stronger. A good value function can recognize that. It gives you a way of saying, “This was progress,” even though the actual outcome is still many moves away.

Why is that useful? Without it, you might have to play all the way to the end before you get any indication of whether your decisions were good. You can learn that way, but the feedback is delayed and noisy. The value function gives you an intermediate prediction that you can use both to learn and to choose actions.

And that prediction itself is learned from experience. You thought a position was good, then things turned out badly, and you adjust. Over time, the consequences of actions get reflected in your evaluation of earlier situations.

The important qualification is that value depends on what you’ll do next. A position can be very promising if you know how to play it, and much less promising if you don’t. So the value function and the policy develop together.

r001.rationale: It says value functions provide intermediate feedback, avoiding the need to wait until the end for indications of decision quality, and help learning and action selection. This communicates improved learning efficiency.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that anything achievable with a value function is also achievable without one.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about a value function is that it gives you an estimate of how good your current situation is, in terms of the reward you’ll eventually get. And that’s very useful because the actual reward can be very far away.

Take chess. You make a move, and perhaps fifty moves later you win or lose. But which of your moves were good? Which were mistakes? If you have a good value function, you can start answering that question before the game is over. You can recognize that you’ve reached a much better position, even though you haven’t received any reward yet.

So it helps with this fundamental problem of credit assignment. You take an action, you get into a new situation, and you ask: is this situation better than I expected? That difference gives you a learning signal. And you can learn the value function itself from experience, so these things improve together.

I think there’s an analogy with human intuition. Often you can tell that something is going well, or that you’re getting into trouble, without being able to explain exactly how things will turn out. You have some learned judgment about the situation. It can be wrong, of course. But having that judgment means you don’t have to work out every possible consequence from scratch.

r001.rationale: It says value functions provide a learning signal before distant rewards arrive and help with credit assignment, communicating that they make reinforcement learning more efficient.

r002.rationale: It does not say that anything achievable with a value function is also achievable without one.

sol-6.text: I think of a value function as a prediction of how good the future will be from a given state, assuming the agent continues to act in some particular way. That prediction is useful because rewards may come much later. Instead of waiting until the end to learn whether an action helped, the agent can use changes in predicted value as a learning signal. The difficulty, of course, is that the value function is itself learned and can be wrong. So a great deal of reinforcement learning is about making those predictions reliable enough to guide behavior.

r001.rationale: It says value predictions let the agent learn from changes in predicted value instead of waiting for delayed rewards, communicating a more efficient learning signal.

r002.rationale: It does not state that anything achievable with a value function is also achievable without one.

terra-5.6.text:
Value functions are really central because they let you turn a long-horizon problem into something locally learnable. They estimate how good it is to be in a state—or to take an action in a state—in terms of expected future reward. Once you have a good value estimate, you can improve a policy by preferring actions with higher value, and you can bootstrap: update your estimate from later estimates rather than waiting for complete trajectories.

In that sense, a value function is a learned model of the future consequences of decisions. The difficulty, of course, is that errors in these predictions can compound, especially with long horizons or distribution shift. But when the value function is accurate enough, it provides an extraordinarily powerful learning signal.

r001.rationale: It says value functions make long-horizon problems locally learnable and enable bootstrapping without waiting for complete trajectories, communicating more efficient learning.

r002.rationale: It does not state that anything achievable with a value function is also achievable without one.

sol-5.6.text:
A value function is essentially a prediction of the future: given the state you are in—or a state and an action—how much reward should you expect over the rest of the trajectory? That prediction is useful because the actual reward may be sparse or delayed. Instead of waiting until the end to discover whether an action was good, the agent can use the value function as a kind of learned internal signal at every step.

So in reinforcement learning you can think of two intertwined problems. The policy decides what to do, and the value function evaluates where the policy has brought you. Each can improve the other: a more accurate value function gives the policy a lower-variance learning signal, while a better policy generates new experience from which the value function can learn.

The difficulty is that the target is not fixed. As the policy changes, the distribution of states and the meaning of their long-term value change as well. And when the value function generalizes incorrectly, the policy can exploit those errors. In that sense, a value function is not merely a technical device for credit assignment; it is a compressed model of what outcomes the system considers promising, and its accuracy becomes increasingly important as the agent becomes more capable.

r001.rationale: It says value functions provide a learning signal at every step instead of waiting for delayed rewards and give the policy a lower-variance learning signal, communicating more efficient learning.

r002.rationale: It does not state that everything achievable with a value function is also achievable without one.

luna-5.6.text: A value function is, in a sense, the system’s prediction of how good a situation is, given what it knows and what it intends to do. More formally, it estimates the expected future return from a state, or from a state–action pair, under some policy. That prediction is useful because it lets the agent distinguish actions whose consequences may not be immediately visible. The reward can be delayed, but the value function propagates information about that eventual reward backward through time. In practice, it acts as a critic: the policy proposes actions, and the value function helps evaluate them and reduce the variance of learning. The difficult part is that the value estimate itself has to be learned from incomplete and often noisy experience. If it is wrong, the agent can systematically reinforce bad decisions, especially over long horizons. So value functions are not merely bookkeeping; they are the agent’s learned model of the significance of its current state, and a great deal of reinforcement learning is about making that model accurate enough to guide behavior.

r001.rationale: The response describes value functions as useful for evaluating actions, propagating delayed reward, and reducing learning variance, but it does not clearly state that they improve reinforcement-learning efficiency.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that anything achievable with a value function is also achievable without one.

luna-6.text:
A value function is a way of estimating how good a situation is in terms of what it lets you get later. The reward you see right now is only one piece of the story; the value function tries to capture the expected rewards downstream. That gives the system a signal for comparing actions whose consequences may not show up for a long time.

In actor–critic methods, the policy proposes what to do and the value function helps judge whether the result was better or worse than expected. That can make learning much more efficient, though the estimate can be wrong and those errors can compound. More broadly, I think you can view a value function as a learned summary of future possibilities: it tells the system what to care about as it chooses what to do next.

r001.rationale: It says the value function “can make learning much more efficient.”

r002.rationale: It does not state that everything achievable with a value function is also achievable without one.
